_README: HUMAN-VERIFIED RFC seed manifest (2026-10-02).
This file exists because AUTOMATED subject auditing of RFC citations did
not converge, and shipping an unvalidated checker would be worse than
having none. Five implementations were tried; each produced a plausible
string and a wrong verdict:
1. first-non-numeric-line  -> 'Network Working Group' for every RFC  (false clean)
2. HTML <title>             -> rfc-editor serves text/plain for .html  (false clean)
3. header-block fallback    -> author names, flagged CORRECT cites    (false positives)
4. abstract first clause    -> 'This document describes...'          (false positives)
5. index regex              -> matched <rfc-entry> inside <obsoleted-by>, checked 2 of 9 (false clean)
So every RFC seed below was verified BY HAND against the document's own
header block. The two genuine defects that audit found are recorded in
`replaced` and must never be reintroduced.
RESOLVED 2026-10-31: the condition in residual_risk is discharged. A
sixth implementation -- tools/audit_rfc_subjects.py -- takes each RFC's
title from the RFC Editor's OWN INDEX (the publisher's index, not the
document body), which is why it does not reproduce failures 1-5: none of
those read the index, and all of them read a page that either serves
text/plain or buries the title under a two-column author block.
It is a PROTOCOL test, not a word test. RFC 4459's title contains the
word 'tunneling', so a word-match accepts it for `tunneling_pivoting`; a
protocol-match asks whether the title names a tunnelling PROTOCOL
(IPsec, VPN, GRE, SSH, L2TP), and it does not.
`python tools/audit_rfc_subjects.py --self-test` now discharges the
both-directions condition ON THIS FILE: all 8 `verified` entries must
PASS and both `replaced` entries must FAIL. MEASURED 2026-10-31: 10/10.
